records.name: Round Half to Even (Banker's) vs Round Half Up / Half Away from Zero

interpretation.python_behavior: Built-in round(x, n) uses ROUND_HALF_EVEN (ties round to nearest even digit). Example: round(2.5) == 2, round(3.5) == 4.
interpretation.sas_behavior: SAS ROUND(argument, round-off-unit) uses ROUND_HALF_AWAY_FROM_ZERO. Example: ROUND(2.5, 1) == 3, ROUND(3.5, 1) == 4.
interpretation.sql_behavior: Standard SQL ROUND(val, d) rounds half away from zero. Example: ROUND(2.5) == 3.
interpretation.javascript_behavior: Math.round(x) rounds towards +infinity on ties (e.g. Math.round(-2.5) == -2, Math.round(2.5) == 3).

risks: Migrating SAS or SQL reports with monetary sums to Python round() causes total variances because Python round(2.5) is 2 instead of 3
validation_rules: In Python, to replicate SAS/SQL round-half-up, use: decimal.Decimal('2.5').quantize(Decimal('1'), rounding=decimal.ROUND_HALF_UP)

records.name: Binary Floating-Point Decimal Representation Artifacts

interpretation.description: Numbers like 0.1, 0.05, 1.15 cannot be represented exactly in IEEE 754 binary floating point. 1.15 is internally 1.14999999999999991118...
interpretation.consequence: round(1.15, 1) in Python yields 1.1 because the internal float is slightly less than 1.15, failing the half-way threshold.

risks: Unexpected rounding results even when code appears mathematically sound
validation_rules: Never perform rounding operations on float for financial or accounting values; convert to Decimal first

records.name: Explicit Truncation (int, math.trunc, SAS INT)

interpretation.python_int: int(2.9) == 2, int(-2.9) == -2 (truncates fractional digits towards zero).
interpretation.equivalence: Python math.trunc() is equivalent to SAS INT() and C++ (int) cast.

risks: Confusing math.floor with int() or SAS INT for negative numbers
validation_rules: Verify negative number handling when converting truncation functions
